messages.content:
Compute the largest positive integer \( n \) such that

\[
n \text{ divides } (\lfloor \sqrt{n} \rfloor)!^{n!} + 450.
\]

Put your final answer within \boxed{}.

message.content:
Let \(k=\lfloor \sqrt n \rfloor\). We analyze the prime power divisors of \(n\).

For a prime power \(p^a \mid n\):

- If \(p \le k\), then \(p \mid k!\), so \(p^{n!}\mid (k!)^{n!}\). Since \(p^a\le n\) and \(n!\ge a\), we get \(p^a \mid (k!)^{n!}\). Thus
\[
p^a \mid 450.
\]
So such prime powers can only come from \(450=2\cdot 3^2\cdot 5^2\).

- If \(p>k\), then \(p^2>n\), so \(a=1\). Also \(\gcd(k!,p)=1\), and since \(p\le n\), we have \(p-1\mid n!\). By Fermat’s little theorem,
\[
(k!)^{n!}\equiv 1 \pmod p.
\]
Thus \(p\mid 450+1=451=11\cdot 41\). So such a prime can only be \(11\) or \(41\), and at most one such prime can divide \(n\).

Hence \(n\) has the form
\[
n=qm,
\]
where \(m\mid 450\), and \(q\in\{1,11,41\}\), with \(q>k\) if \(q>1\).

Now bound the possibilities:

- If \(q=1\), then \(n=m\le 450\).
- If \(q=11\), then \(k\le 10\), so \(n=11m<121\), giving \(m\le 10\). The largest divisor of \(450\) at most \(10\) is \(10\), so \(n\le 110\).
- If \(q=41\), then \(k\le 40\), so \(n=41m<1681\), giving \(m\le 40\). The largest divisor of \(450\) at most \(40\) is \(30\), so
\[
n\le 41\cdot 30=1230.
\]

It remains to check that \(n=1230\) works. Here
\[
\lfloor\sqrt{1230}\rfloor=35,
\]
and
\[
1230=30\cdot 41.
\]

Since \(30\mid 35!\), we have \(30\mid (35!)^{1230!}\), and also \(30\mid 450\), so
\[
30 \mid (35!)^{1230!}+450.
\]

For the factor \(41\), note that \(40\mid 1230!\) and \(\gcd(35!,41)=1\), so
\[
(35!)^{1230!}\equiv 1 \pmod{41}.
\]
Thus
\[
(35!)^{1230!}+450\equiv 1+450=451\equiv 0 \pmod{41}.
\]
Since \(30\) and \(41\) are coprime, \(1230\) divides the expression.

Therefore the largest such integer is

\[
\boxed{1230}
\]
